challenges.name: Ten Clear
challenges.note: Ten correct actions in a row

hazards.solo-worksite: You are working without a second person in sight. Track protection is never a one-person job — the lookout exists because you cannot watch the line and do the work at the same time, and an ANSI/ISEA-rated hi-vis vest does nothing for a worker that nobody is actually watching for.
hazards.third-rail: That is the traction current rail. Isolation confirmed elsewhere does not matter here until you have proven this section dead — it carries enough current to kill on contact, no arc required.
hazards.unmarked-boundary: That limit of possession has no board. Without a marked boundary a train movement has no way to know where your protection actually ends.
hazards.unprotected-crossing: You crossed the running line without the lookout's clearance. A train at line speed covers that distance faster than you can react to a warning.

interrupts.alert: The isolator lamp has gone back to red. Traction current is in this section again and your hands are on the bonding clamp.
interrupts.cue: Your lever is still off. The current did not come from your lever.
interrupts.missNote: You carried on bonding a joint on a re-energised conductor rail. Seven hundred volts DC needs no arc and gives no warning: it is a contact injury, at the hand already on the clamp, and the lookout is the only person who would have seen it happen.
interrupts.why: An isolation is a shared state, not a switch position. Your isolator is one end of a section that can be fed from the other, and the only thing holding the far end open is the signaller knowing there are people between your boards. So when the current comes back with your own lever still off, the answer is not the lever — it is the one voice that can reach whoever closed it. You call, you say where your people are, and nothing touches that rail again until the far end is confirmed open and your own tester says so.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not what gets the current off. Your own isolator is already open — this one has to go to the signaller.

interrupts.alert: Your lookout has turned away and started walking up the cess. Nobody is watching the line and you are kneeling between the rails with a gauge in both hands.
interrupts.cue: Protection here is a person, and the person has stopped doing it.
interrupts.missNote: You finished the gauge measurement with nobody watching the line. In fog, kneeling inside the four foot, every part of that job was resting on a warning that was not coming, and the first thing that would have told you is the one that arrives far too late to use.
interrupts.why: A lookout is not a formality standing near the job — they are the arrangement under which one person is permitted to face away from the line at all. The sighting distance on the briefing sheet is worked back from line speed so that a warning arrives with enough seconds in it to stand, turn and get clear, and every one of those seconds assumes somebody is looking. The moment the protection lapses the work stops. You do not finish the measurement first, because the measurement is exactly how long you would not have seen the train.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not what protects you out here. Stop, and get the lookout back on the line before another reading is taken.

lateNotes.left-tool: Nothing gets tallied against a list until the pack-up walk is actually done.
lateNotes.new-fastener: That fastener doesn't get swapped in until the defective one is off and the seat is clean.
lateNotes.rail-clamp: Nothing gets clamped to the rail before possession is confirmed and the current is proven off.
lateNotes.track-gauge: Track geometry is measured after possession is secured, never while trains could still be moving.

name: Track Access

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the possession plan: limits, isolation, lookout arrangement.
steps.prompt: Read the possession plan: limits, isolation, lookout arrangement.
steps.title: Attend the possession briefing
steps.why: Everyone on site works to the same plan under FRA roadway worker protection rules at 49 CFR Part 214. A worker who missed the briefing does not know where the protection actually starts and ends, and the crew has no way to know that they do not know.

steps.cue: Confirm with the signaller that possession is granted for this section.
steps.prompt: Confirm with the signaller that possession is granted for this section.
steps.title: Take possession from the signaller
steps.why: Until the signaller says the words that grant it, the section is still open to traffic as far as the signalling system is concerned, regardless of what the engineering schedule says should be happening. Possession is a spoken confirmation you can quote back, not an assumption drawn from a timetable.

steps.cue: Swing the traction power isolator for this section fully over to OFF.
steps.prompt: Swing the traction power isolator for this section fully over to OFF.
steps.title: Isolate the traction current
steps.why: The isolator is what removes the current, but the switch position alone is not proof of anything — that comes at the next step. It goes fully over, too: a lever left part way across its travel is a lever that has not actually broken the circuit, whatever the handle looks like from the cab.

steps.cue: Test the rail with the approved tester and commit when it reads safe.

gauge.label: TRACTION RAIL — VOLTAGE
gauge.missNote: Still live. Confirm the isolation point with the signaller before touching the rail.

steps.prompt: Test the rail with the approved tester and commit when it reads safe.
steps.title: Prove the traction rail is dead
steps.why: The same rule as any other isolation: measured with an approved tester, never assumed from a switch position or a control-room readout. Seven hundred volts DC through a conductor rail gives no warning and needs no arc to kill, so a reading near zero is the only thing that makes the rail approachable at all.

steps.cue: Place a boundary board at each end of the worksite.

itemNames.board-a: limit of possession board — up end
itemNames.board-b: limit of possession board — down end

steps.prompt: Place a boundary board at each end of the worksite.
steps.title: Mark the limits of possession
steps.why: The boards are the only thing a train crew, a signaller or another gang can actually see from a moving vehicle that marks where your protection begins and ends — everything past a board is a section that still runs to normal rules.

steps.cue: Position the lookout with a clear sighting distance both ways.
steps.prompt: Position the lookout with a clear sighting distance both ways.
steps.title: Post the lookout
steps.why: The lookout's only job is watching the line in both directions and giving a warning early enough for the gang to clear it, coordinated the same way a SMART-represented train crew coordinates a move through a work zone. Sighting distance is calculated back from line speed, not chosen for convenience.

steps.cue: Clamp the bond across the joint before working on it.
steps.prompt: Clamp the bond across the joint before working on it.
steps.title: Fit the rail bonding clamp
steps.why: The bond maintains the signalling circuit's continuity across the joint you are about to work on, so the interlocking upstream still sees an occupied or clear track correctly instead of losing the detection the moment the rail is broken.

steps.cue: Set the gauge across the rails and commit inside tolerance.

gauge.label: TRACK GAUGE
gauge.missNote: Outside tolerance for this class of track. Log the defect and adjust before handback.

steps.prompt: Set the gauge across the rails and commit inside tolerance.
steps.title: Measure track gauge
steps.why: Standard gauge is held to a tight tolerance for a reason: outside it, a wheel flange stops following the rail head and starts climbing it under load, which is how a slow, boring maintenance defect turns into a derailment nobody saw building.

steps.cue: Carry the new fastener from the tool chest to the worn one and set it in place.

drag.missNote: Not seated on the sleeper — carry it over to the worn fastener and set it square.

steps.prompt: Carry the new fastener from the tool chest to the worn one and set it in place.
steps.title: Replace the defective fastener
steps.why: A loose fastener lets the rail move under load, and the failure is progressive: a little play becomes a lot of play as every axle passing over it works the hole a fraction wider. Fixed now, with the seat clean and the new fastener carried across and seated square, it is a five-minute job. Missed, or set crooked because it was rushed, it is a derailment risk that starts as a barely audible click under a slow-moving inspection car.

steps.cue: Scan the worksite and pick out anything that didn't make it back into the kit before the tally is called complete.

itemNotes.left-tool: Caught before pack-up closed out — a wrench left in the four foot is exactly the kind of foreign object the tally exists to catch.

steps.prompt: Scan the worksite and pick out anything that didn't make it back into the kit before the tally is called complete.
steps.title: Walk the site for anything left behind
steps.why: A tool left on the track is a foreign object under the next train — caught in a set of points it derails a movement, and lying on the running rail it becomes a projectile under a wheel at line speed. The tally is counted out and counted back against the list every time, but the list only catches what somebody actually walked the site to find; it does not walk itself.

steps.cue: Close the isolator once everyone is clear of the rail.
steps.prompt: Close the isolator once everyone is clear of the rail.
steps.title: Restore traction current
steps.why: Confirmed clear of the rail, then and only then re-energised. The sequence never reverses.

steps.cue: Confirm with the signaller that the line is clear and possession is given up.
steps.prompt: Confirm with the signaller that the line is clear and possession is given up.
steps.title: Hand possession back
steps.why: The section stays under your protection until you formally hand it back. Walking away without the call is how a possession never actually closes.
